{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Robert Hermann Breusch''' (April 2, 1907 – March 29, 1995) was an American [[number theory|number theorist]], the William J. Walker Professor of Mathematics at [[Amherst College]].<ref name="mm">{{citation|contribution=Robert Breusch|title=Memorial Minutes|publisher=[[Amherst College]]|url=https://www.amherst.edu/academiclife/provost_dean_faculty/facmeetings/memorialminutes#Breusch|access-date=2010-04-24|first1=David|last1=Armacost|first2=James|last2=Denton|first3=Robert|last3=Romer|first4=Dudley|last4= Towne}}.</ref><ref name="dmv">[https://www.dmv.mathematik.de/die-dmv/105-kurzbiographien/402-kurzbiographien-b-bi-bz.html Brief biography] (in German), [[German Mathematical Society]], retrieved 2010-04-24.</ref>

Breusch was born in [[Freiburg]], [[Germany]], and studied mathematics both at the [[University of Freiburg]] and the [[University of Berlin]].<ref name="mm"/><ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|name=Robert Breusch|id=19951}}.</ref> Unable to secure a university position after receiving his doctorate, Breusch became a schoolteacher near Freiburg, where he met his future wife, Kate Dreyfuss; Breusch was Protestant, but Dreyfuss was Jewish, and the two of them left Nazi Germany for [[Chile]] in the mid-1930s.<ref name="mm"/><ref>{{citation|title=Mathematicians fleeing from Nazi Germany: individual fates and global impact|first=Reinhard|last=Siegmund-Schultze|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2009|isbn=978-0-691-14041-4|page=131}}.</ref> They married there, and Breusch found a faculty position at [[Federico Santa María Technical University]] in [[Valparaíso]].<ref name="mm"/> In 1939, they left Chile for the United States, inviting [[Robert Frucht]] to take Breusch's place at Santa María;<ref name="gg">[http://sansanos.us/pictures/Profesores/Dr.RobertoFrucht.html Biography of Frucht] (in Spanish), Walter Gaete and Raúl González, retrieved 2010-04-22.</ref> after some years working again as a schoolteacher, Breusch found a position at Amherst College in 1943. He became the Walker professor in 1970, and retired to become an emeritus professor in 1973.<ref name="mm"/><ref name="dmv"/> The Robert H. Breusch Prize in Mathematics, for the best senior thesis from an Amherst student, was endowed in his memory.<ref name="mm"/>

As a mathematician, Breusch was known for his new proof of the [[prime number theorem]]<ref name="mm"/><ref>{{citation|title=Another proof of the prime number theorem|first=R.|last=Breusch|journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]|volume=21|issue=1|pages=49–53|year=1954|doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-54-02106-7|mr=0068567}}.</ref> and for the many solutions he provided to problems posed in the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]''.<ref name="mm"/> His thesis work combined [[Bertrand's postulate]] with [[Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions]] by showing that each of the progressions 3''i''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, 3''i''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2, 4''i''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, and 4''i''&nbsp;+&nbsp;3 (for ''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, 1, 2, ...) contains a [[prime number]] between ''x'' and 2''x'' for every ''x''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;7.<ref name="mg"/><ref>{{citation|first=R.|last=Breusch|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|title=Zur Verallgemeinerung des Bertrandschen Postulates, daß zwischenx und 2x stets Primzahlen liegen|language=German|volume=34|issue=1|year=1932|pages=505–526|doi=10.1007/BF01180606|s2cid=121351858}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|contribution=On the greatest prime factor of an arithmetical progression|title=A Tribute to Paul Erdős|editor1-first=Alan|editor1-last=Baker|editor2-first=Béla|editor2-last=Bollobás|editor3-first=A.|editor3-last=Hajnal|first1=T. N.|last1=Shorey|first2=R.|last2=Tijdeman|pages=385–390|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1990|isbn=978-0-521-38101-7}}.</ref> For instance, he proved that for n > 47 there is at least one prime between n and (9/8)n. He also wrote a [[calculus]] textbook, ''Calculus and Analytic Geometry with Applications'' (Prindle, Weber & Schmidt, 1969) with [[C. Stanley Ogilvy]].
